????  shared_from_this is already in the bind_front call.
Yes, but `this` may be dangling if the shared object is deleted before the bound-callback is invoked.
But the shared_ptr is bound to the handler by value, so how could it be deleted before the bound callback?
Can you provide the test you used for this?  It's still not clear to me how this commit would change, but maybe there's something in the test that gives a hint.

the relationship between objects are:

```
HttpClient
  └─> unordered_map<string, shared_ptr<ConnectionPool>>
        └─> ConnectionPool
              └─> vector<shared_ptr<ConnectionInfo>>
                    └─> ConnectionInfo (with async handlers)
```

The coredump occurred at:
```
  ConnectionInfo::afterRead() - connPolicy->invalidResp(respCode)
```

Or, potentionally on the other callbacks (I think I saw this/similar one before [during the dev time - esp. resHandler() part])

```
- ConnectionInfo::afterRead()   callback(parser->keep_alive(), connId, res);
- ConnectionInfo::waitAndRetry() - callback(false, connId, res);
- ConnectionInfo::afterSendData() - resHandler(res);
```


The problem potentially may occur:

- The callback member variable holds a std::function
  that may capture references to objects in the ConnectionPool or HttpClient.

- If the ConnectionPool or HttpClient is destroyed while async operations are
  pending, the callback may reference destroyed objects [1][2][3].

- The shared_from_this() pattern keeps ConnectionInfo alive
  but doesn't protect objects captured by the callback.

Some links discuss about the similar topics.
[1] https://stackoverflow.com/questions/26397269/what-if-a-basic-waitable-timer-is-destructed-when-there-are-still-async-operatio
[2] https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/latest/doc/html/boost_asio/overview/core/cancellation.html
```
Cancellation requests should not be emitted during an asynchronous operation's initiating function. Cancellation requests that are emitted before an operation starts have no effect. Similarly, cancellation requests made after completion have no effect.
```
[3] https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/latest/doc/html/boost_asio/overview/core/cancellation.html


For example, ConnectionInfo::callback may still be invoked even if its object is destroyed.

If so, the callback (invalidResp()) from this usage seems invalid.

```
boost::beast::http::async_read(
    conn, buffer, thisParser,
    std::bind_front(&ConnectionInfo::afterRead, this, shared_from_this()));
```


Unfortunately, the problem seems not easily reproducible.

I think it is because the async operation may need to be occurred
at a very specific timing and pushed into the io_context queue
during the object destruction time.
(I'm not also able to reproduce it).

The high-level reproduction sequence may look like

- Create a HttpClient (ConnectionPool & ConnectionInfo).
- An async operation (e.g. read) is started.
  (Note: however, it is queued into io_context, but not yet executed)

- HttpClient is destroyed (ConnectionPool/ConnectionInfo also destroyed)
  and all asyncs are cancelled.
  The async operation was already in io_context, its callback may still be invoked.

As the solution, the associated object (e.g. ConnectionInfo)'s lifetime would need
to be kept as long as the callback is needed.
(i.e. object is captured and kept as long as io callbacks are needed).

---

To reproduce it, I think - some kind of the low-level delay injection at IO-layer & boost-code so that the async operations are held on io_context queue during the object destruction, but it seems not easy.

----
Perhaps, for the future thinking, [2] suggests to use `boost::asio::bind_cancellation_slot()` approach to deal with async cancellation (i.e. timer.cancel() or async call cancel()) properly.

[2] https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/latest/doc/html/boost_asio/overview/core/cancellation.html

----
Until then, I think semantically, capturing 'object' as a whole in lambda (instead of passing both `this` & `shared_ptr` to the function which may later invoke callback) seems more consistent (in making sure the same value).

I add the observation (from the actual production code) into the commit msg.

It tells that this problem may occur if the object (shared_from_this) is already deleted before the callback (which is bound to std::bind_front) is yet invoked.
Then, the value of `this` (which was passed to std::bind_front) may be dangling when the callback is invoked.

```
The std::bad_function_call exception means connPolicy->invalidResp is an empty std::function.
```

The cause is that ConnectionInfo object (this) is already destroyed when
afterRead is called, leading to accessing correupted memory.
```

This analysis doesn't seem correct.  If the std::function is empty, it shouldn't be null, it should be uncallable.  This is also tracking bind_front, not std::function.

I meant -
The "this" is captured at the bind time of std::bind_front(). 
Even if shared_ptr is already destroyed before afterRead() is invoked, the value of "this" (which was captured at the time bind) of afterRead() may become invalid (as it is not the value of *shared_ptr(), but a previously captured "this" value).
Then any reference to connPolicy may be invalid (or null) and thus invalidResp() could also be a bad_function.

both "this" and "shared_from_this()" are captured in the bind_front call.  This is a pattern we do a lot.  Because the shared_ptr is passed to the callback function, the shared_ptr MUST be valid at the time the callback is called (otherwise what would it call with?)

This is why I don't understand the statement that shared_from_this() Isn't captured.
why did we change this?  Old one looks more correct.
I've updated the commit message to show what we observed in the actual production code.
